sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Network troubleshooting is a disciplined process. The exam tests which step should happen next—not merely whether a technical action could eventually solve the problem.
bullets: Establish a theory of probable cause
Plan a solution and identify potential effects
Verify full functionality and apply preventive measures
sections.callout: IDENTIFY → THEORIZE → TEST → PLAN → FIX → VERIFY → DOCUMENT

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: Read the scenario for what the technician has already done. That tells you which methodology step comes next.
bullets: Prove or disprove the cause → Test
Choose the repair and consider impact → Plan
Confirm the whole service works → Verify
Record findings, actions, outcomes, and lessons learned → Document

sections.title: Step 1 — Identify the Problem
paragraphs: Begin by defining the real problem before changing anything. Gather objective evidence and learn what the user experienced.
bullets: Gather information from users, monitoring systems, logs, and documentation
Question users about timing, scope, frequency, and impact
Determine whether anything changed before the issue began
Duplicate the problem, if possible, without creating additional risk
Approach multiple problems individually so unrelated symptoms do not blur the diagnosis
sections.callout: Collect facts first. A symptom is evidence—not yet the root cause.

sections.title: Step 2 — Establish a Theory of Probable Cause
paragraphs: Use the evidence to form a likely explanation. Question the obvious before assuming a rare failure.

entries.title: Bottom-to-Top OSI
paragraphs: Start with physical connectivity and move upward. This is effective when link, power, cabling, or interface symptoms are likely.

entries.title: Top-to-Bottom OSI
paragraphs: Start with the application and move downward. This is effective when the physical network appears healthy but a user-facing service fails.

entries.title: Divide and Conquer
paragraphs: Begin at a middle layer, test, and use the result to decide whether to move up or down.
entries.memoryHook: Split the stack and narrow the search.

sections.title: Step 3 — Test the Theory to Determine the Cause
paragraphs: Run a focused, safe test that can confirm or reject the suspected cause.
bullets: If the theory is confirmed, determine the next steps needed to resolve the problem
If the theory is not confirmed, establish a new theory or escalate
sections.callout: A theory is a suspected cause. A test provides evidence.

entries.title: Establish a Plan of Action
paragraphs: Choose the corrective action and identify potential effects such as downtime, dependencies, security impact, rollback needs, and required approval.
entries.memoryHook: Know the blast radius before touching production.

entries.title: Implement or Escalate
paragraphs: Perform the approved solution when it is within your authority and capability. Escalate when risk, access, expertise, or policy requires another owner.
entries.memoryHook: Execute safely—or hand it to the right tier.

sections.title: Step 6 — Verify Full System Functionality
paragraphs: Do more than confirm the original symptom disappeared. Test the complete service, related functions, and user experience.
bullets: Confirm the repair solved the reported problem
Check that dependent and adjacent services still operate
Have the user validate when appropriate
sections.callout: A successful change is not complete until the system is verified.

sections.title: Step 7 — Document Throughout the Process
paragraphs: Record findings, actions, outcomes, and lessons learned throughout the process. Good documentation supports handoffs, repeatability, trend analysis, and faster future troubleshooting.

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Question users or determine changes → Identify
Suspect a likely cause → Establish a theory
Run a targeted diagnostic → Test the theory
Start in the middle → Divide and conquer

entries.title: Identify vs. Theory
paragraphs: Collecting facts and symptoms is identification. Naming a probable cause is establishing a theory.

entries.title: Theory vs. Test
paragraphs: A theory is the hypothesis. A diagnostic action that proves or disproves it is the test.

entries.title: Plan vs. Implement
paragraphs: Considering impact and choosing the fix is planning. Performing the fix is implementation.

entries.title: Implement vs. Verify
paragraphs: Making the change is implementation. Confirming complete operation afterward is verification.

entries.title: Bottom-to-Top vs. Top-to-Bottom
paragraphs: Start at cabling/link for bottom-to-top; start at the application for top-to-bottom.

entries.title: Documentation Timing
paragraphs: Do not wait until the very end to capture evidence. The objective explicitly requires documentation throughout the process.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: Middle then narrow → Divide and conquer
sections.callout: IDENTIFY → THEORIZE → TEST → PLAN → FIX → VERIFY → DOCUMENT
